paper_title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Text-to-image (T2I) generation maps natural-language descriptions to images. Modern T2I systems have an ingrained reliance on internet-scale language pretraining 1 for semantic conditioning of image generators. This dependence is realized via two designs, distinguished by how and when text tokens interact with image tokens: (1) Late fusion, the predominant design, uses two separate models: large model is pretrained on text, and the resulting text embeddings are used to condition separate image generator through crossor joint attention (Saharia et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2025; Zhao et al., 2026); (2) Early fusion removes the separate text encoder while retaining language pretraining within single multimodal model trained on text-only and image-text data, with captions used as prefix to condition image generation (Team et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Across both designs, language pretraining dominates the compute budget, accounting for over 80% of total pretraining FLOPs in representative T2I systems (Sun et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026). This raises two issues. First, its contribution to T2I generation has not been systematically quantified. Second, language pretraining cost is often excluded, understating the total cost of building T2I system. In this work, we show that strong T2I generation can be achieved without language pretraining. We introduce Halcyon, family of early-fusion autoregressive models that learn text conditioning directly from imagetext pairs using next-token prediction. We quantify the contribution of language pretraining to T2I generation using GPIC (Chandrasegaran et al., 2026), dataset of 100M image text pairs, through three experimental axes: (1) From-scratch pretraining: we train all components from scratch, including the text and image tokenizers and the generative model; (2) Data composition and scheduling: under fixed pretraining budget, we control the mixture and schedule of textonly, T2I, and I2T examples and measure their effect on T2I generation quality; and (3) Compute comparisons: we pretrain representative T2I baselines on GPIC and compare generation quality as function of total pretraining compute, decomposed into language and vision. Through these experiments, we quantify the utility of language pretraining for T2I generation. Our results show that Halcyon achieves strong T2I generation without language pretraining, with generation Frechet distance (gFD) consistently improving as model size scales (Figure 1). Particularly, Halcyon-0.52B achieves 48.0 gFD, outperforming LlamaGen-XL/8 (FLAN-T5-XL 1.22B + 0.90B image generator; 63.3 gFD) using 18.2 less total pretraining compute. Halcyon-1.6B achieves 35.3 gFD, outperforming JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (Qwen3-1.7B + 1.10B image generator; 41.0 gFD) using 275 less total pretraining compute. Our data composition and scheduling experiments further show that external text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Further, we show that Halcyon can learn image captioning by replacing caption-dropped T2I examples with I2T sequences, while maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We provide simple recipe for pretraining T2I models without language pretraining. Our work prompts rethinking the role of generic language pretraining for multimodal generation. sections.content: 1010 109 Modern T2I systems use large-scale language pretraining through two designs. In late fusion, the predominant paradigm, language model is pretrained separately on text-only data, and its embeddings condition visual generator. sections.content: pretraining is incorporated into multimodal pretraining. Chameleon (Team et al., 2024a), Transfusion (Zhou et al., 2025), and Emu3 (Wang et al., 2026) train jointly on text-only and imagetext data, while Tuna-2 (Liu et al., 2026) and SimpleAR (Wang et al., 2025) initialize from pretrained Qwen models. Figure 2 compares the text and vision tokens used to pretrain these T2I systems. Systems with language pretraining consume 1012 1014 text tokens, often exceeding the vision budget. In contrast, Halcyon uses no text-only language pretraining; its only language supervision comes from caption tokens paired with images, more than two orders of magnitude lower than the language-pretraining budgets shown. We note that early T2I systems such as DALL-E, CogView, and GLIDE learned text conditioning directly from paired imagetext data, without language pretraining (Ramesh et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2021; Nichol et al., 2022). However, the role of language pretraining has been debated: Imagen (Saharia et al., 2022) found benefits from scaling pretrained text encoders, whereas Parti (Yu et al., 2022) found that text-encoder pretraining only marginally reduced T2I generation loss. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2024) found limited benefits from initializing autoregressive T2I models with pretrained language models. Nevertheless, modern T2I systems have largely shifted toward pretrained language models for text conditioning. We quantify the role of language pretraining and show that T2I models trained entirely from scratch, without language pretraining, can outperform strong T2I baselines relying on language pretraining.

sections.title: 3 APPROACH
sections.content: Halcyon is decoder-only Transformer with joint textimage vocabulary. We model text and image tokens as single sequence using next-token prediction, following prior multimodal earlyfusion works (Team et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2026). All components, including the text tokenizer, image tokenizer, and multimodal generative model are trained from scratch. Below, we describe the tokenizers, sequence format, training objective, and pretraining data composition and scheduling.

sections.title: 3.1 TOKENIZATION
sections.content: Images. We train discrete image tokenizer on GPIC images, following the encoderdecoder design of Cosmos Tokenizer (Agarwal et al., 2025) with finite scalar quantization (FSQ) (Mentzer et al., 2024). The tokenizer downsamples images by factor of 8 along each spatial dimension, with codebook size of 64,000. Each 256 256 image is represented as = 1,024 image tokens = (x1, . . . , xN ) obtained by flattening the 32 32 grid in raster order. Text. We train byte-level BPE tokenizer (Sennrich et al., 2016) from scratch on GPIC captions and OpenWebText Gokaslan & Cohen (2019), with vocabulary size of 16,384. Each caption is represented as = (c1, . . . , cL). Joint vocabulary. Text tokens, image tokens, and special tokens form single vocabulary of size 80,640, comprising 16,384 text tokens, 64,000 image tokens, and 256 special tokens. The model uses shared embedding table and output head. We use [SOV] and [EOV] to mark the beginning and end of an image, [EOS] to mark the end of sequence, and [PAD] for sequence padding.

sections.content: We use four sequence formats for pretraining shown in Figure 3. Text-only sequences are packed, while image-containing sequences are padded to fixed length with [PAD] tokens. sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Dataset and pretraining protocol. We pretrain on GPIC (Chandrasegaran et al., 2026), dataset of approximately 100M imagetext pairs, at 256 256 resolution. All configurations are trained for one epoch on GPIC with global batch size of 1,024 and an identical warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule (Hu et al., 2024a). For language pretraining, we use ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2025) packed without padding. Model details and training details are provided in Appendix A. Tokenizer training and evaluation. Image tokenizer. We train our image tokenizer for one epoch using reconstruction and perceptual losses, followed by an additional half epoch with adversarial loss using PatchGAN discriminator. Compared to Cosmos-DI-8x8 (Agarwal et al., 2025), we increase the decoder width from 128 to 192. To assess reconstruction quality, we compare our tokenizer with pretrained LlamaGen-VQ16x16 and Cosmos-DI-8x8 tokenizers. We include Real-vs-Real scores as reference. Our tokenizer outperforms CosmosDI-8x8 across all metrics  (Table 1)  . As with prior discrete tokenizers, reconstruction fidelity is lower for small text and fine glyphs (Team et al., 2024a; Sun et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025). Late fusion is the predominant design choice for modern T2I systems. Selecting baselines for this study is non-trivial: existing systems differ in pretraining objective, language conditioning, image representation, and training setup, while our study requires public pretraining code and models that enable controlled interventions to study the role of language pretraining. We select two representative families, LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024) and JiT-T2I (Li & He, 2026; Ma et al., 2026). They cover (i) autoregressive and diffusion-based generation, (ii) encoder-decoder and decoder-only language models of different sizes, and (iii) image sequence lengths of 256 and 1,024. For both families, we use the authors official codebases and follow their training configurations unless stated otherwise. Below, we describe our setup and summarize them in Table 3. LlamaGen (Sun et al., 2024). This method uses FLAN-T5-XL text encoder for language modeling, discrete image tokenizer, and an autoregressive image generator. Default (LlamaGen-XL). We use the original LlamaGen configuration: FLAN-T5-XL, the pretrained image tokenizer producing 256 image tokens from codebook of 16,384 entries, and the 0.78B image generator. Use Halcyon image tokenizer (LlamaGen-XL/8). Starting with the default configuration, we replace the image tokenizer with our GPIC-trained tokenizer. This increases the visual vocabulary size by 4, the image sequence length from 256 to 1,024, and the image generator size from 0.78B to 0.90B. Use smaller text encoder (LlamaGen-XL-T5-Base/8). Starting with LlamaGen-XL/8, we replace FLAN-T5-XL (1.22B) with FLAN-T5-base (0.11B) to study the effect of language model size.

On compositional generation benchmarks, Halcyon-0.52B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ on GenEval (44.9 vs. 43.2) and matches its DPG-Bench score (76.84 vs. 76.85). At 1.6B, Halcyon surpasses JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ on both GenEval (53.5 vs. 43.2) and DPG-Bench (77.9 vs. 76.9). Moreover, Halcyon-1.6B achieves these results with 275 less total pretraining compute than JiT-T2I-XXL/8++. sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: Model scaling and classifier-free guidance. We examine how Halcyon scales from 0.1B to 4B parameters. Figure 7 shows that both image and text validation NLL decrease consistently with model size, with larger models achieving lower NLL throughout pretraining. This demonstrates improvements in modeling both modalities as model capacity increases. We further examine how the optimal CFG scale varies with model size (Figure 8). As model size increases from 0.1B to 4B, the guidance scale minimizing gFD on GPIC Validation-50K decreases from 7.5 to 4.5, while gFD improves from 142.7 to 28.4. This suggests that larger models require less guidance to achieve their best generation quality, although CFG remains beneficial across all evaluated model sizes. Figure 7: Scaling behavior of Halcyon across model sizes. Validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) for image tokens (left) and text tokens (right) throughout pretraining on GPIC. As model size increases from 0.1B to 4B, both image and text NLL consistently decrease, with larger models achieving lower NLL throughout training. All models are pretrained from scratch under the same training schedule.

sections.content: Caption length and text conditioning. Since Halcyon learns text conditioning directly from paired imagetext data, we investigate how generation quality varies with the length of the caption. We evaluate all five model sizes using short, medium, and long captions from GPIC Test-1M  (Table 10)  . As model size increases from 0.1B to 4B, gFD decreases across all caption lengths. Medium and long captions consistently achieve lower gFD than short captions. These results suggest that more detailed text descriptions improve T2I generation quality, although longer captions do not consistently outperform medium-length captions. The optimal scale drops from 7.5 (0.1B) to 4.5 (4B) as gFD improves from 142.7 to 28.4; these scales are used on Test-50K. Implications of language pretraining for T2I generation. Our results challenge the prevailing reliance on internet-scale language pretraining for T2I generation. In late-fusion systems, pretrained language models provide text representations, but the image generator must learn to map these representations to images using paired data. On GPIC Test-50K captions, FLAN-T5-XL achieves lower caption NLL than FLAN-T5-Base (2.76 vs. 3.24, averaged over three instruction prompts), with 13.5 more language-pretraining compute (Chung et al., 2024). Yet, using FLAN-T5-XL instead of FLAN-T5-Base only modestly improves LlamaGen gFD (66.7 63.3). This result is consistent with Parti (Yu et al., 2022), which reported marginal benefits from text-encoder pretraining. For early-fusion models, text-only pretraining optimizes p(T ), whereas T2I generation requires learning p(I ) with image tokens produced by an independently trained tokenizer. Strong text-only modeling therefore does not guarantee useful initialization for image generation. Consistent with this view, our randomly initialized Qwen3 model achieves lower vision validation NLL throughout pretraining (Appendix Figure 10) and lower final gFD than its language-pretrained counterpart. In contrast, Halcyon learns text representations for image generation jointly from paired imagetext data without language pretraining, although our experiments do not isolate the effect of joint training. Since our study focuses on pretraining, we account for all pretraining FLOPs required to build each T2I system, including language-model, image-tokenizer, and image-generator pretraining. We note that our study examines the role of language pretraining in lateand earlyfusion systems, not the relative capabilities of autoregressive and diffusion-based image generators. Beyond T2I, our findings motivate reconsidering the role of modality-specific pretraining in other multimodal settings, including biological data (Radical Numerics, 2026; Neiswanger et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Limitations and future directions. While our experiments use GPIC, which is, to our knowledge, the largest high-quality, centrally hosted, publicly available dataset and benchmark for visual generation, extending these findings to other datasets and higher resolutions remains important. Our controlled data composition and scheduling experiments use Halcyon-0.52B, while the pretrained initialization comparison uses Qwen3-0.6B; extensions to larger model sizes and pretraining budgets would help establish the generality of our findings. Although our late-fusion baselines include

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: diffusion-based generators, our controlled interventions focus on autoregressive models. Extending these experiments to Transfusion-style models (Zhou et al., 2025) is valuable direction. Finally, text-to-video systems such as Wan (Wan et al., 2025), CogVideoX (Yang et al., 2025b), and Mochi (Team, 2024) also rely on large pretrained language encoders for video generation. Investigating whether T2V models can learn text conditioning directly from paired videotext data, without language pretraining, is promising direction toward efficient video generation systems. Conclusion. In this work, we study whether internet-scale language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduced Halcyon family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models trained entirely from scratch on paired imagetext data (GPIC). Our models outperform strong late-fusion baselines while using significantly less total pretraining compute. Our controlled experiments show that external text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation under the evaluated settings. Furthermore, replacing caption-dropped T2I examples with I2T supervision enables image captioning while maintaining competitive generation quality under the same pretraining budget. Our results show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our work studies text-to-image generative modeling, which can be used to generate realistic visual content and may therefore be misused. By providing significantly lower-cost recipe for training strong T2I models, our work lowers the barrier to developing capable generative systems, including for malicious use. Halcyon and the baseline models are pretrained on GPIC and may inherit biases or limitations present in its images and captions. Our work does not involve human-subject studies or the collection of new dataset. We do not identify additional ethical risks specific to our method beyond those associated with visual generative models.

sections.title: B SAMPLING DETAILS
sections.content: All models generate one 256 256 image per caption using the GPIC Test-50K set. For Halcyon, we sample 1,024 image tokens autoregressively after the caption prefix and [SOV], using temperature 1.0 with top-k and top-p disabled and fixed seed. CFG is applied only to imagetoken logits, ℓcfg = ℓu + γ(ℓc ℓu), where the unconditional branch uses the [SOV] prefix without the caption. For each model size, we select γ to minimize gFD on the GPIC validation set (Figure 8). Baselines. For LlamaGen and JiT-T2I, we use the official sampling code and settings and identify the optimal CFG setting using the GPIC validation set.

sections.title: C ADDITIONAL RESULTS
sections.content: C.1 PER-CATEGORY RESULTS ON GENEVAL AND DPG-BENCH Tabs. 18 and 19 report per-category GenEval and DPG-Bench results for all models in Tab. 5. GenEval overall scores are reported as mean std. We additionally report Halcyon trained with I2T supervision (pdrop=0.0, η=0.1) at every scale. On GenEval, I2T supervision matches the standard recipe at all model sizes, with differences in overall scores within one standard deviation. On DPG-Bench, it yields slightly higher overall scores for four of the five model sizes.
